Sample text:
---
# A-440

The deafness came for the high notes first, which was God's idea of a joke. Forty years of leaning into pianos, right ear to the soundboard, and the frequencies that lived there — the sizzle of a just-struck note, the glassy overtone that told you a unison was clean — packed up and left. The audiologist showed him the graph, the line falling off a cliff past four thousand hertz. She said *sensorineural*, *noise-induced*, *typical for your profession*, as if tuning pianos were a rumor he'd heard about himself.

People think tuning is about hearing. It isn't, or not only. It's about the beats. Strike two strings nearly in tune and the sound swells and ebbs, swells and ebbs, a slow knocking, a fist on a door. When the knocking stops, the strings agree. Elias Voss had spent a lifetime listening for the end of that knocking, and a body remembers. He could feel beats in his teeth. In the bones of his wrist against the keybed. Once, tuning a concert grand, he'd felt a slow beat in his sternum and known the tenor section was a cent and a half flat.

So when the school called — Roosevelt Middle, music room B, an old upright that had outlived four music teachers and a flood — he said yes. His wife, Dana, said, "Elias." Just that. They'd had the conversation in the winter, when he'd announced his retirement the way you announce a death in the family: with casseroles and too much eye contact.

The piano was a Vose, 1954, a studio upright, walnut veneer gone cloudy at the corners. The music room smelled of radiators and old felt. The teacher was young — Ms. Okafor, cardigan, coffee, apologies. "It's mostly for the kids to bang on," she said. "I didn't think you'd come. My cousin said you don't do schools anymore."

"I don't," Elias said. He set down his case. "I do this one."

He opened the piano and the smell came up: dust, iron, fifty years of felt. Inside, the plate was stamped with a slogan, SOMETHING FOR EVERY GENERATION, which the flood had edited to SOMETHING FOR EVERY GENERA—.

He worked from the middle outward, the way you calm a room. Temperament first, F to F, the founding compromise: a piano cannot be perfect and honest at once, so you spread the error around until nobody can point at one interval and cry. Fifths a hair flat, fourths a hair wide. He struck the fork against his knee — A-440, the note the whole world agrees on — and built the octave, then the fifths inside it, listening for the third that should beat just so. The major third, F to A, wants to be pure and never is, not on a piano, and that is the whole tragedy and mercy of the instrument.

He set the pins the old way, with a test blow, striking each key hard enough to seat the string against the bridge, because a piano tuned only for the tuning room falls apart by Thursday. He had tuned for concert halls and funerals, for a president once, and for a woman who wanted hers a half-step sharp because her dead husband had liked it that way and she was not ready for the house to agree with her.

The kids came and went, period by period, a zoology of elbows. A boy played a bass line from a video game, over and over, the way boys do, not badly. A girl with braids sat down while he was muting the treble and asked if he was a doctor. "Of pianos," he said. She considered this. "My grandmother's piano is sick," she said. "It coughs." He said he'd make a house call if she ever brought the address, and she wrote it on his invoice in pencil, backwards, so he had to hold it to the window.

By afternoon his right ear was a seashell and his left was doing the work of two, angled in, and he was tuning the last unisons in the treble by vibration alone, two fingers on the plate, waiting for the buzzing to stop. A unison, when it locks, doesn't just sound still. It feels still. The note gets heavier, somehow, more itself. He had a theory he'd never told anyone: you don't tune a string to a pitch, you tune it to its life, to the pitch it would have if it were alone in the universe and completely honest. The treble was old and false, the strings grooved by a million hammer blows, and no amount of turning would make them ring like new. So he tuned them to what they still could be, which was not nothing.

Ms. Okafor locked the door behind last period and sat down while he packed. She played, hesitantly, a Chopin waltz, the E-minor one, the one everyone starts and never quite finishes. She finished it. The piano was not a good piano. It would not be a good piano tomorrow. But for a minute the room had a center, a stillness, the way a snow globe has a stillness when you set it down.

"Elias," she said, reading it off his case, "is it in tune?"

He considered the question the way he used to, when clients asked it in front of company, as if tuning were a light switch. "It's in tune with itself," he said. "That's the best any of them get."

Outside, Dana was double-parked with the hazards on. He put the case in the trunk, the fork last — except that he didn't. In the family way, he left it on the piano, A-440, brass and dark with thumbprints, for the girl with braids. She'd find it Monday. She'd wonder.

He got in the car. His ears were ringing the way they always did after, a sound with no source, a note that wasn't there and would never stop. Dana pulled out. Behind them the school windows went gold with the late sun, and if a piano was playing he couldn't say. He felt it anyway, faintly, through the seat, through the floor of the world: something for every generation, still holding its breath, still almost, nearly, in tune.
---
